question: What happens to a suspended complaint under the Canada Labour Code once the employee has taken the required measures?
answer:
## Suspension of Complaint and Subsequent Actions

### Section 251.02: Canada Labour Code - Suspension of Complaint | Assistance — Head

This section outlines the process for suspending a complaint under the Canada Labour Code. It states:
"The suspension ends when, in the Head’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

This indicates that once the employee fulfills the required measures outlined in the notice issued by the Head, the suspension of the complaint ceases. The complaint is then no longer suspended and can proceed further.

### Section 241.1: Canada Labour Code - Division XIV - Unjust Dismissal: Suspension of complaint

This section also addresses the suspension of complaints, stating:
"The suspension ends when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

This reinforces the principle that the suspension ends upon the completion of the required measures, as determined by the relevant authority (either the Head or the Board).

### Section 246.2: Canada Labour Code - Division XIV.1-Complaints Relating to Reprisals: Suspension of complaint

This section mirrors the previous ones, stating:
"The suspension ends when, in the Board’s opinion, the measures specified in the notice have been taken."

This consistency across different sections of the Canada Labour Code confirms that the completion of the required measures is the trigger for the end of the suspension.

question: How does the Canada Labour Code protect an employee's right to receive wages from their employer in the context of other legal provisions?
answer:
## Protection of Employee's Right to Receive Wages Under Other Legal Provisions

### Section 131 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 131 explicitly addresses the relationship between compliance with the Canada Labour Code and an employee's right to compensation under other laws. It states:
"Section 131 The fact that an employer or employee has complied with or failed to comply with any of the provisions of this Part may not be construed as affecting any right of an employee to compensation under any statute relating to compensation for employment injury or illness, or as affecting any liability or obligation of any employer or employee under any such statute."

This section is crucial because it clarifies that adherence to, or non-adherence to, the Canada Labour Code does not impact an employee's entitlement to compensation under other statutes, such as those dealing with employment injuries or illnesses. This ensures that an employee's fundamental right to receive compensation for such events remains protected, regardless of any issues arising under the Canada Labour Code itself.

### Section 146.5 Regarding Attendance at Board Proceedings

Section 146.5 outlines the right of an employee to be compensated for time spent attending Board proceedings:
"Section 146.5 An employee who is a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1) and who attends at the proceeding, or any employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding and who attends, is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work."

This provision directly protects an employee's right to receive wages even when they are required to attend Board proceedings. It ensures that employees are not financially penalized for participating in legal processes related to their employment. The section explicitly states that the employee is entitled to be paid at their "regular rate of wages" for the time spent at the proceeding, which would otherwise have been considered "time at work." This guarantees that employees are not financially disadvantaged for fulfilling their legal obligations.

### Labour Standards Legislation in Quebec and Yukon

While not directly part of the Canada Labour Code, the Labour Reports document highlights how provincial and territorial labour standards legislation further protects employees. It notes:
"Quebec Legislation - Act respecting  labour standards Definition “Employee” means a person who works for an employer and who is entitled to a wage and also includes a worker who is party to a contract, under which he or she..."

This definition emphasizes that an employee is entitled to a wage, and the definition extends to workers who are party to a contract. This reinforces the fundamental right of employees to receive compensation for their work, regardless of the specific nature of their employment arrangement.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code, through sections like 131 and 146.5, and complemented by provincial labour standards legislation, provides multiple layers of protection for an employee's right to receive wages. These provisions ensure that compliance with the Code does not affect other compensation rights, and that employees are compensated for time spent fulfilling legal obligations related to their employment.

question: Are there any exceptions to the typical rules governing when a trade union can apply for certification, particularly when a collective agreement is in place?
answer:
## Exceptions to Certification Application Rules

### Application for Certification: Exception (Section 24.1)

Section 24.1 of the Canada Labour Code provides a specific exception to the typical rules governing when a trade union can apply for certification.
"A trade union that is not certified but has entered into a collective agreement the term of which has not expired may, despite paragraphs 24(2)(c) and (d), make an application for certification at any time, in respect of the unit to which the collective agreement applies or substantially the same unit."

This section allows a trade union that has already reached a collective agreement, even if it isn't yet certified, to apply for certification at any time. This overrides the usual restrictions outlined in paragraphs 24(2)(c) and (d), which specify limitations based on the duration of the collective agreement. This exception is crucial because it provides a pathway for unions to seek formal certification even when a collective agreement is already in effect, potentially streamlining the process and ensuring the union's representation is recognized.



### Application for Certification: Where Certification Prohibited (Section 24)

While not an exception to the timing of application, Section 24 outlines situations where certification is prohibited, which indirectly affects when a union *can* apply.
"The Board shall not certify a trade union as, and a trade union shall not act as, the bargaining agent for both a bargaining unit comprised of private constables and a bargaining unit comprised of employees other than private constables if any or all of the employees in both such bargaining units are employed by the same employer."

This section prevents a union from representing two distinct bargaining units if they overlap in terms of employees. This means that a union cannot apply for certification for both units simultaneously if there is an overlap in employees. This limitation impacts the timing of applications, as a union must first address the certification for one unit before applying for the other.

### Application for Certification: Limitation (Section 24)

Section 24 also includes limitations on when a union can apply for certification based on the duration of an existing collective agreement.
"(b) where no collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force but a trade union has been certified under this Part as the bargaining agent for the unit, after the expiration of twelve months from the date of that certification or, with the consent of the Board, at any earlier time; (c) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of not more than three years, only after the commencement of the last three months of its operation; and (d) where a collective agreement applicable to the unit is in force and is for a term of more than three years, only after the commencement of the thirty-fourth month of its operation and before the commencement of the thirty-seventh month of its operation and, thereafter, only (i) during the three month period immediately preceding the end of each year that the collective agreement continues to operate after the third year of its operation, and (ii) after the commencement of the last three months of its operation."

This section dictates specific timeframes for applying for certification depending on whether a collective agreement is already in place and its duration. For example, if a collective agreement is in force for a term of not more than three years, a union can only apply for certification after the last three months of its operation. This limitation directly affects the timing of applications, requiring unions to wait until a specific point in the collective agreement's term before seeking formal certification.

question: Can an employer take disciplinary action against an employee who has exercised their rights under the Canada Labour Code, and if so, under what circumstances?
answer:
## Employer Disciplinary Action and Employee Rights under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 147: General Prohibition on Disciplinary Action

Section 147 of the Canada Labour Code establishes a general prohibition against employers taking disciplinary action against employees for exercising their rights under the Code.
"...or take any disciplinary action against or threaten to take any such action against an employee because the employee (a) has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding taken or an inquiry held under this Part; (b) has provided information to a person engaged in the performance of duties under this Part regarding the conditions of work affecting the health or safety of the employee or of any other employee of the employer; or (c) has acted in accordance with this Part or has sought the enforcement of any of the provisions of this Part."

This section clearly states that an employer cannot take disciplinary action against an employee for engaging in activities protected by the Labour Code. These protected activities include testifying in legal proceedings, providing information regarding workplace health and safety, or exercising rights under the Code.

### Section 147.1: Exception for Willful Abuse of Rights

However, Section 147.1 provides an exception to this general prohibition. It allows an employer to take disciplinary action against an employee who has "wilfully abused" their rights under sections 128 and 129.
"An employer may, after all the investigations and appeals have been exhausted by the employee who has exercised rights under sections 128 and 129, take disciplinary action against the employee who the employer can demonstrate has wilfully abused those rights."

This exception is not a blanket permission to discipline employees. The employer must demonstrate that the employee's exercise of their rights was a willful abuse, implying a deliberate and unreasonable misuse of those rights. Furthermore, the employer must follow all investigation and appeal processes before taking disciplinary action.

In summary, while Section 147 generally prohibits disciplinary action against employees exercising their rights under the Canada Labour Code, Section 147.1 allows for disciplinary action in cases of willful abuse of those rights, provided certain conditions are met.

" (no source found for the quotation)Subject to subsections 134.1(7) and 135(10) and any regulations made under subsection 135.2(1), a committee shall establish its own rules of procedur in respect of the terms of office, not exceeding two years, of its members and the time, place and frequency of regular meetings of the committee and may establish any rules of procedur for its operation that it consideers advisable."

question: How do changes in business activities or ownership affect the continuity of labour relations, collective agreements, and dispute resolution processes under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Successor Rights and Obligations: Impact of Business Changes

The Canada Labour Code addresses the continuity of labour relations, collective agreements, and dispute resolution processes when there are changes in business activities or ownership through Section 44, 46, 47, and 51. These sections outline the rights and obligations of parties involved in such transitions.

### Section 44: Definitions and Continuity Upon Business Transfer

Section 44 defines "business" broadly, encompassing
"...any federal work, undertaking or business and any part thereof..." It also defines "sell" to include the transfer or disposition of a business, with leasing being considered a sale for the purposes of the Code. This broad definition is crucial for determining when the Code applies to a business transfer.

The section then details the impact of a business sale on existing labour relations. It states:
"Where an employer sells a business, (a) a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent; (b) a trade union that made application for certification in respect of any employees employed in the business before the date on which the business is sold may, subject to this Part, be certified by the Board as their bargaining agent; (c) the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that is, on the date on which the business is sold, applicable to the employees employed in the business; and (d) the person to whom the business is sold becomes a party to any proceeding taken under this Part that is pending on the date on which the business was sold and that affects the employees employed in the business or their bargaining agent."

This means that upon a business sale, the existing union remains the bargaining agent, and the buyer assumes responsibility for the existing collective agreement. Furthermore, any ongoing legal proceedings related to the employees or their union continue under the Code with the new owner as a party.

### Section 46 & 47: Successor Rights and Obligations

Sections 46 and 47 deal with successor rights and obligations, particularly in the context of federal public administration. Section 46 states that the Board must determine any questions arising under Section 44, including the identity of the purchaser of a business. This ensures clarity regarding the successor employer's responsibilities.

Section 47 specifically addresses situations where a portion of the federal public administration is transferred to a corporation or business. It clarifies that collective agreements continue in force until their expiration date, subject to certain conditions. It also states:
"(8) An arbitral award that is continued in force by virtue of subsection (1) is deemed to be (a) part of the collective agreement for the bargaining unit to which the award relates, or (b) where there is no collective agreement for the bargaining unit, a collective agreement for the bargaining unit to which the award relates for the purposes of section 49, and this Part, other than section 80, applies in respect of the renewal or revision of the collective agreement or entering into a new collective agreement."

This provision ensures that arbitral awards are treated as part of the collective agreement, even after a change in ownership or business structure.

### Section 51: Technological Change and Collective Agreements

Section 51 addresses the impact of technological change on collective agreements. It outlines conditions under which the application of sections 52, 54, and 55 (related to technological change) does not apply. This section highlights the importance of negotiation and agreement between the employer and the union to address the effects of technological changes on employment terms and conditions.
"Where an employer sells a business, (a) a trade union that is the bargaining agent for the employees employed in the business continues to be their bargaining agent; (b) a trade union that made application for certification in respect of any employees employed in the business before the date on which the business is sold may, subject to this Part, be certified by the Board as their bargaining agent; (c) the person to whom the business is sold is bound by any collective agreement that is, on the date on which the business is sold, applicable to the employees employed in the business; and (d) the person to whom the business is sold becomes a party to any proceeding taken under this Part that is pending on the date on which the business was sold and that affects the employees employed in the business or their bargaining agent."

This demonstrates that even with a sale, the existing collective agreement remains in effect, and the new owner is obligated to uphold its terms.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code provides a framework for ensuring continuity of labour relations, collective agreements, and dispute resolution processes when businesses change ownership or activities. The Code prioritizes the rights of existing unions and the continuation of existing agreements, while also addressing the responsibilities of new owners and the need for negotiation in the face of technological change.

question: How are alternative holidays with pay typically arranged for employees when a general holiday falls on a non-working day, and what factors influence the scheduling of these alternative holidays?
answer:
## Alternative Holiday Arrangements When a General Holiday Falls on a Non-Working Day

### General Policy for Non-Working Days
"Except as otherwise provided by this Division and subject to subsection (2), when a general holiday falls on a day that is a non-working day for an employee, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay at some other time, which may be by way of addition to his annual vacation or granted as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer."

This section of the Canada Labour Code outlines the standard procedure when a general holiday coincides with a day an employee would normally not be working. The core principle is that the employee is entitled to a holiday with pay, but it is to be scheduled at a mutually agreeable time.

### Factors Influencing Scheduling

The scheduling of these alternative holidays is influenced by several factors, as detailed in the "canada.ca" document:

**1. Mutual Agreement:
"...as a holiday with pay at a time convenient to both the employee and the employer." This highlights that the scheduling is ideally determined through a collaborative process between the employee and employer.

**2. Specific Holiday Exceptions:
"...when New Year’s Day, Canada Day, National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Remembrance Day, Christmas Day or Boxing Day falls on a Sunday or Saturday that is a non-working day, the employee is entitled to and shall be granted a holiday with pay on the working day immediately preceding or following the general holiday." This provides a specific rule for certain holidays, mandating the holiday be given on the immediately preceding or following working day.

**3. Collective Agreements:
"...subject to a collective agreement, there must be a written agreement on the substitution between the:  employer union, and employee(s)..."  Collective agreements often contain specific provisions regarding the substitution or rescheduling of holidays.

**4. Individual Employee Requests:
"You may also request to substitute a general holiday with another day as part of your request for flexible work arrangements. This request must be authorized by your employer in writing." Employees can also propose alternative arrangements, subject to employer approval.

**5. Notice Requirements for Substitution:
"The employer must post the notice of substitution for at least 30 days before it takes effect..." If an employer wishes to substitute a holiday for another day, they must provide adequate notice to employees.

In summary, alternative holidays with pay are typically arranged through a combination of mutual agreement, adherence to specific rules for certain holidays, and the potential influence of collective agreements and individual requests. The scheduling process aims to ensure the employee receives the holiday pay while accommodating the operational needs of the employer.

question: What are the consequences for a complainant if the Board decides to suspend or reject their complaint under the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Suspension of Complaint

### Section 251.02 (Canada Labour Code)
"If the Head is satisfied that the employee must take measures before the Head may continue to deal with the complaint made under section 251.01, the Head may, at any time, suspend consideration of the complaint, in whole or in part."

This section outlines the process for suspending a complaint. The Head of the relevant body (likely the Board, based on other sections) has the authority to suspend consideration if they believe the complainant needs to take certain actions first. 

### Section 246.2 (Canada Labour Code)
"If the Board suspends a complaint, the Board shall notify the employee in writing and specify in the notice (a) the measures that the employee must take; and (b) the period of time within which the employee must take those measures."

This section details what happens when a complaint is suspended. The Board is required to provide written notification to the complainant, clearly stating the measures the complainant must take and the timeframe for doing so.

### Section 246.3 (Canada Labour Code)
"If the Board rejects a complaint, it shall notify the employee in writing, with reasons."

This section explains the consequences of the Board deciding to reject a complaint. The Board is obligated to inform the complainant in writing and provide the reasons for the rejection.

## Rejection of Complaint

### Section 246.3 (Canada Labour Code)
"The Board may reject a complaint made under subsection 246.1(1), in whole or in part, (a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the employee, (iv) there are other means available to the employee to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator..."

This section outlines the grounds on which the Board can reject a complaint. These include situations where the complaint falls outside the Board's jurisdiction, is frivolous or made in bad faith, has already been settled, or has been adequately addressed through other legal avenues.

### Section 241.2 (Canada Labour Code)
"The Board may reject a complaint referred to it under subsection 241(3), in whole or in part, (a) if the Board is satisfied that (i) the complaint is not within its jurisdiction, (ii) the complaint is frivolous, vexatious or not made in good faith, (iii) the complaint has been settled in writing between the employer and the complainant, (iv) there are other means available to the complainant to resolve the subject matter of the complaint that the Board considers should be pursued, or (v) the subject matter of the complaint has been adequately dealt with through recourse obtained before a court, tribunal, arbitrator or adjudicator..."

This section mirrors the grounds for rejection outlined in Section 246.3, but applies to complaints referred to the Board under a different division of the Canada Labour Code (Division XIV-U unjust dismissal).

In summary, if the Board suspends a complaint, the complainant must take specified actions within a given timeframe. If the Board rejects a complaint, the complainant will receive written notification with the reasons for the rejection.

question: What are the requirements for a conciliation board to proceed with a sitting when one of its members is absent?
answer:
## Requirements for a Conciliation Board Sitting with an Absent Member

### Section 85(2) - Quorum and Absence

Section 85 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the requirements for a conciliation board to proceed with a sitting when a member is absent.
"The chairperson and one other member of a conciliation board constitute a quorum but, in the absence of any member, the other members shall not proceed unless the absent member has been given reasonable notice of the sitting."

This section establishes that a quorum consists of the chairperson and one other member. However, it explicitly states that if a member is absent, the remaining members *cannot* proceed with the sitting unless the absent member has received reasonable notice. This implies that the board must ensure the absent member is informed of the sitting and given an opportunity to participate, even if they are physically absent. The definition of "reasonable notice" is not provided in this section, leaving it open to interpretation based on the circumstances.

answer:
## Authority to Appoint in Case of Vacancy

### Section 217: Head's Appointment in Lieu of Failed Appointments

Section 217 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the process when a trade union or redundant employees fail to appoint a member to the joint planning committee as required by sections 214 and 215.
"If a trade union fails, or redundant employees fail, to appoint a member to a joint planning committee as provided in sections 214 and 215, the Head may, on application of any redundant employee, appoint a member to the committee in lieu of that trade union or those employees, as the case may be, and that member is a representative of the redundant employees represented by the trade union or of the redundant employees who failed to appoint the member, as the case may be."

This section explicitly grants the Head the authority to appoint a member in lieu of a failed appointment by either a trade union or the redundant employees themselves. This appointment is made upon the application of any redundant employee. The appointed member will represent the redundant employees who either the trade union represents or those who failed to make an appointment. Therefore, the Head has the authority to fill the vacancy and ensure the committee remains constituted.

question: What are the specific timelines and processes that a trade union or a corporation/business must follow when applying for certification or an order related to collective agreements or arbitral awards after a portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes part of a corporation or business?
answer:
## Timeline and Processes for Certification/Orders After Public Administration Change

This analysis details the timelines and processes for trade unions and corporations/businesses when dealing with collective agreements or arbitration awards following a change in the structure of the federal public administration. The information is derived from sections 47 and 33 of the Canada Labour Code.

### Section 47: General Procedures Following Administrative Changes

Section 47 outlines the procedures that apply when a portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes part of a corporation or business.

#### Continuation of Existing Agreements
"...a collective agreement or arbitral award that applies to any employees in that portion of the federal public administration and that is in force at the time the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of such a corporation or business continues in force, subject to subsections (3) to (7), until its term expires..."

This indicates that existing collective agreements and arbitration awards are initially maintained. The continuation is subject to further processes outlined in subsequent subsections.

#### Application for Certification (Trade Union)
"A trade union may apply to the Board for certification as the bargaining agent for the employees affected by a collective agreement or arbitral award referred to in subsection (1), but may so apply only during a period in which an application for certification of a trade union is authorized to be made under section 24."

This establishes a limited window for a trade union to apply for certification after the administrative change. The application must be made during a period when certification applications are generally permitted.

#### Application for an Order (Corporation/Business or Bargaining Agent)
"...during the period beginning on the one hundred and twentieth day and ending on the one hundred and fiftieth day after the date on which the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part..."

This subsection specifies a 30-day window (120th to 150th day) for the corporation or business, or a bargaining agent, to apply for an order. This application aims to determine the appropriate bargaining units and the designated bargaining agent.

#### Board Determination and Potential for Notice to Bargain
"Where the Board determines, pursuant to paragraph (4)(c), that a collective agreement or arbitral award shall remain in force, either party to the collective agreement or arbitral award may, not later than sixty days after the date the Board makes its determination, apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve on the other party a notice to bargain collectively."

Following the Board's determination on whether an agreement remains in force, there is a 60-day window for either party to request permission to issue a notice to bargain collectively.

#### Further Application for Notice to Bargain
"Where no application for an order is made pursuant to subsection (3) within the period specified in that subsection, the corporation or business, as employer of the employees, or any bargaining agent bound by a collective agreement or arbitral award that, by subsection (1), is continued in force, may, during the period commencing on the one hundred and fifty-first day and ending on the two hundred and tenth day after the date the portion of the federal public administration is established as or becomes a part of the corporation or business, apply to the Board for an order granting leave to serve on the other party a notice to bargain collectively."

If no application for an order is made within the initial 30-day window, a second 30-day window (151st to 210th day) opens for the corporation or business or bargaining agent to request permission to issue a notice to bargain collectively.

### Section 33: Certification of Bargaining Agents and Related Matters

Section 33 addresses the certification of bargaining agents when a union applies for certification in a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers' organization.

#### Designation of Employers' Organization
"Where a trade union applies for certification as the bargaining agent for a unit comprised of employees of two or more employers who have formed an employers’ organization, the Board may designate the employers’ organization to be the employer if it is satisfied that each of the employers forming the employers’ organization has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable it to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer under this Part."

This section outlines the process for designating an employers' organization as the employer in a collective bargaining context.

#### Inclusion of New Members
"The Board may, on application by the employers’ organization, include in the designation referred to in subsection (1) any employer that becomes a member of the employers’ organization if it is satisfied that that employer has granted appropriate authority to the employers’ organization to enable the employers’ organization to discharge the duties and responsibilities of an employer and that such an inclusion would ensure the fulfilment of the objectives of this Part."

This allows for the addition of new members to an employers' organization, which could impact the bargaining unit and the certification process.

#### Impact on Collective Agreements
"...this Part applies to the interpretation and application of any collective agreement or arbitral award affected thereby."

This clarifies that the rules of this part of the code apply to collective agreements and arbitration awards when an employers' organization is designated as the employer.

These sections highlight the complexities involved in managing collective agreements and arbitration awards when the structure of the federal public administration changes. The timelines and processes are designed to ensure a smooth transition and to protect the rights of both employees and employers.

question: Can the Board's determination of a question regarding a business sale or change in business activity be considered final and binding?
answer:
## Board Determination of Business Sale/Activity: Finality and Binding Nature

### Section 46 - Board's Authority to Determine Questions

Section 46 of the Canada Labour Code explicitly states:
"The Board shall determine any question that arises under section 44, including a question as to whether or not a business has been sold or there has been a change of activity of a business, or as to the identity of the purchaser of a business."

This section establishes the Board's authority to resolve disputes concerning business sales and changes in activity, as defined in Section 44. The use of the word "shall" indicates a mandatory obligation for the Board to make a determination.

### Section 156 - Finality of Board Orders and Decisions

Section 156 of the Canada Labour Code addresses the finality of Board orders and decisions. It states:
"Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

This provision directly addresses the question of whether the Board's determination regarding a business sale or change of activity is final and binding. The statement that
"...final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court." strongly suggests that the Board's determination is not subject to judicial review. This means that once the Board makes a determination on whether a business has been sold or has undergone a change in activity, that determination is considered conclusive and cannot be challenged in court.

### Section 20(2) - Finality of Decisions

Section 20(2) further reinforces the finality of decisions made by the Board:
"A decision referred to in subsection (1) is, except as stipulated by the Board, final."

This section clarifies that decisions made by the Board, including those related to the questions outlined in Section 46, are generally final. The exception allows for potential reconsideration by the Board itself, but it does not provide a basis for external legal challenge.

In conclusion, based on Sections 46, 156, and 20(2) of the Canada Labour Code, the Board's determination of a question regarding a business sale or change in business activity is considered final and binding, as it is not subject to review in any court.

question: How do leaves of absence under Division VII or VIII, or certain specified absences, affect an employee's vacation plans according to the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Impact of Leaves of Absence on Vacation Plans

### Section 187.1: Interrupting Vacation for Leaves of Absence

Section 187.1 of the Canada Labour Code outlines the conditions under which an employee can interrupt their vacation. It states:
"An employee may interrupt a vacation granted to them under this Division in order to permit them to take a leave of absence under Division VII or VIII or section 247.5 or to be absent due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1)."

This section directly addresses the question by explicitly stating that an employee *can* interrupt their vacation to take a leave of absence under Division VII or VIII, or for other specified absences. This means that vacation plans are not necessarily inflexible and can be adjusted to accommodate these other obligations.

### Marginal Note 187.1: Application of section 209.1

The marginal note associated with section 187.1 further clarifies the application of this interruption. It states:
"If an employee interrupts a vacation to take leave under any of sections 205.1, 206, 206.1 and 206.3 to 206.9 and resumes the vacation immediately at the end of that leave, section 209.1 applies to them as if they did not resume the vacation before returning to work."

This indicates that if an employee takes a leave of absence under specific sections (205.1, 206, 206.1, and 206.3 to 206.9) and immediately resumes their vacation, the interruption is treated as if it never happened for the purpose of applying section 209.1. This provides a mechanism to avoid complications with vacation accrual or other related matters.

### Section 187.2: Postponing Vacation

Section 187.2 provides another avenue for adjusting vacation plans. It allows employees to postpone their vacation:
"Despite paragraph 185(a) or any term or condition of employment, an employee may postpone their vacation until after the day on which a leave of absence taken under Division VII or VIII or section 247.5, or an absence due to a reason referred to in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1), ends."

This section explicitly states that an employee can postpone their vacation if they have taken a leave of absence under Division VII or VIII, section 247.5, or for a reason specified in subsection 239(1) or 239.1(1). This allows for flexibility in vacation scheduling, particularly when dealing with unavoidable absences.

### Section 187.2: Notice to Employer

The section also includes a requirement for notice:
"An employee who intends to postpone their vacation shall, as soon as possible, provide the employer with prior written notice of the postponement."

This ensures that the employer is informed of the change in vacation plans, allowing for appropriate adjustments to staffing and other operational matters.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code provides mechanisms for employees to interrupt or postpone their vacations when required by leaves of absence under Division VII or VIII, section 247.5, or for other specified absences. These provisions offer flexibility and allow employees to balance their work obligations with their vacation plans.

question: What is the general purpose of the regulations that the Governor in Council may make under this section of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## General Purpose of Regulations under Section 264 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 264 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council broad authority to create regulations. The general purpose of these regulations is to facilitate the implementation and administration of the Code's provisions. This includes a wide range of areas related to labour standards and processes.

### Record Keeping and Reporting

One key aspect of the regulations is the requirement for employers to maintain specific records. Section 264(1)(a) states that the Governor in Council may make regulations
"...requiring employers to keep records of wages, vacations, holidays and overtime of employees and of other particulars relevant to the purposes of this Part or any Division thereof..." This indicates a focus on transparency and accountability in employment practices.

Furthermore, the regulations address the information employers must provide to the government. Section 264(1)(a.2) specifies regulations regarding
"...the information that an employer must provide to the Head for the purpose of establishing that the performance of activities referred to in subsection 167(1.2) fulfils the requirements of a program referred to in that subsection, and the circumstances in which an employer must provide it..." This highlights the need for reporting to ensure compliance with specific programs and standards.

### Wage Calculation and Payment

The regulations also cover the calculation and payment of wages. Section 264(1)(d) explicitly states that the regulations can be used
"...for calculating and determining wages received by an employee in respect of his employment, including the monetary value of remuneration other than money and, for the purposes of any provision or provisions of this Part specified in the regulations, the regular rate of wages of employees..." This demonstrates the importance of clear guidelines for wage determination.

### Hours of Work and Conditions

Regulations are also used to establish standards for working hours and conditions. Section 264(1)(f) allows for
"...prescribing the maximum number of hours that may elapse between the commencement and termination of the working day of any employee..." This indicates a focus on worker safety and well-being. Additionally, Section 264(1)(h) mandates that employers must notify employees about various aspects of their work conditions, including
"...the particulars of hours of work, including the hours at which shifts change, (iii) the particulars of rest periods and meal periods..."

### Administrative Procedures

Beyond direct employment standards, the regulations also cover administrative procedures. Section 264(1)(a) grants the power to regulate
"...to or by whom and in what manner any notice, request or report that may be given or made to or received by the Minister shall be given, made or received..." This ensures efficient communication and processing of information related to the Code.

In essence, the regulations under Section 264 serve to provide detailed rules and procedures necessary for the effective implementation and enforcement of the Canada Labour Code, covering areas from record-keeping and wage determination to working conditions and administrative processes.

question: How does the Board ensure that its orders remain relevant and effective in changing circumstances?
answer:
## Review and Amendment Powers of the Board

### Section 18 of the Canada Labour Code

The Board possesses the authority to adapt its orders to evolving circumstances. Section 18 explicitly states:
"The Board may review, rescind, amend, alter or vary any order or decision made by it, and may rehear any application before making an order in respect of the application."

This indicates a proactive approach to ensuring relevance. The Board isn't bound by its initial decisions; it can revisit and modify them as needed. The ability to "review, rescind, amend, alter or vary" demonstrates flexibility. Furthermore, the power to "rehear any application" before making a new order ensures that the Board considers updated information and perspectives when adapting its decisions.

## Appeal Process for Review of Board Decisions

### Section 251.12 of the Canada Labour Code

The appeal process provides a mechanism for external review, which indirectly contributes to the relevance and effectiveness of Board orders. Section 251.12 outlines the powers of the Board in an appeal:
"(1) The Board may, in an appeal under this Part, make any order that is necessary to give effect to its decision, including an order to (a) confirm, rescind or vary, in whole or in part, the decision being appealed..."

This section highlights the Board's ability to "rescind or vary" its own decisions during an appeal. This means that if a party successfully challenges a Board order, the Board can modify or even overturn its previous ruling, ensuring that the order remains aligned with current circumstances and legal interpretations.

## Finality of Orders and Limitations on Review

### Section 22 of the Canada Labour Code

While Board orders are generally final and not subject to court review, there are exceptions. This finality is intended to provide stability and certainty. However, the exceptions ensure that orders can be revisited if necessary.
"(1) Subject to this Part and to any regulations made under paragraph 111.01(1)(g), every order or decision made by the Board under this Part is final and is not to be questioned or reviewed in any court, except in accordance with the Federal Courts Act on the grounds referred to in paragraph 18.1(4)(a), (b) or (e) of that Act."

The exception to the finality of orders, as outlined in Section 22, allows for review in specific circumstances, such as when the order is beyond the Board's jurisdiction. This safeguard ensures that the Board's decisions remain legally sound and relevant to the evolving legal landscape.

## General Finality of Board Decisions

### Section 156 of the Canada Labour Code

This section reinforces the finality of Board decisions.
"(1) Every order or decision made or direction issued by the Board under this Part is final and shall not be questioned or reviewed in any court."

While this section emphasizes the finality of orders, it is important to note that the exceptions outlined in other sections, such as Section 22, provide avenues for review when necessary. This balance between finality and review ensures that the Board's orders remain relevant and effective in changing circumstances.

answer:
## Purpose of Establishing a Joint Planning Committee

The purpose of establishing a joint planning committee is to facilitate cooperation between the employer and redundant employees in developing an adjustment program. This committee serves as a forum for discussion and negotiation regarding the terms of termination and support for affected employees.
"An employer who gives notice to the Head under section 212 must, as soon as possible after giving the notice, establish a joint planning committee consisting of any number of members that is required or permitted by this section and sections 215 and 217."

This quote directly states the requirement for an employer to establish a joint planning committee following notification to the Head. The committee's role is to work towards an adjustment program, which aims to mitigate the negative impacts of group termination on redundant employees.

## Timing of Establishing the Committee

An employer must establish the joint planning committee "as soon as possible after giving the notice" to the Head under section 212.
"The members of a joint planning committee must be appointed and must convene for their first sitting within two weeks after the date of the notice given to the Head under section 212."

This passage clarifies the timeline. While the committee must be established as soon as possible, it must also be appointed and hold its first meeting within two weeks of the notification to the Head. This timeframe allows for the prompt commencement of discussions and the development of an adjustment program.

question: What are the implications and prerequisites for filing an order of the Board in the Federal Court?
answer:
## Filing an Order of the Board in the Federal Court

### Section 23: Filing Requirement and Exceptions

Section 23 outlines the process for filing a Board order or decision in the Federal Court. It states:
"The Board shall, on the request in writing of any person or organization affected by any order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the Federal Court, unless, in the opinion of the Board, (a) there is no indication of failure or likelihood of failure to comply with the order or decision; or (b) there is other good reason why the filing of the order or decision in the Federal Court would serve no useful purpose."

This indicates that the primary prerequisite for filing an order in the Federal Court is a written request from any party affected by the order. The Board is obligated to file a copy of the order, excluding the reasons for the decision, unless it determines that filing would be unnecessary or futile.

### Section 23(2): Board's Obligation to File
"Where the Board files a copy of any order or decision in the Federal Court pursuant to subsection (1), it shall specify in writing to the Court that the copy of the order or decision is filed pursuant to that subsection and, where the Board so specifies, the copy of the order or decision shall be accepted for filing by, and registered in, the Court without further application or other proceeding."

This section clarifies the Board's responsibility when filing. The Board must inform the Federal Court in writing that the filing is being done under Section 23. Once the Board makes this specification, the order is accepted and registered without needing additional procedures.

### Section 23(3): Legal Effect of Registration
"When a copy of any order or decision of the Board is registered pursuant to subsection (2), the order or decision has the same force and effect as a judgment obtained in the Federal Court and, subject to this section and the Federal Courts Act , all proceedings may be taken thereon by any person or organization affected thereby as if the order or decision were a judgment of that Court."

This is a crucial aspect of filing in the Federal Court. Registration of the order grants it the same legal force as a judgment issued by the Federal Court. This means that any legal proceedings related to the order can be initiated in the Federal Court as if it were a judgment of that court. This significantly enhances the enforceability of the Board's decision.

### Section 23.1: Filing in Provincial Superior Court (Optional)
"The Board may, on application by a person or organization affected by an order or decision of the Board made under this Part, file a copy of the order or decision, exclusive of reasons, in the superior court of a province. Section 23 applies, with any modifications that the circumstances require, to an order or decision filed in such a superior court."

This section provides an alternative to filing in the Federal Court. The Board can file the order in a provincial superior court upon application from an affected party. Importantly, Section 23 applies to such filings, meaning the same requirements and legal effects would apply, with any necessary adjustments for the provincial court system.

question: What happens to the Minister's powers of appointment under the Act when they are delegated to another person?
answer:
## Delegation of Ministerial Powers

### Section 140: General Delegation Provisions

Section 140 outlines the general framework for the Minister's ability to delegate their powers, duties, and functions.
"Subject to any terms and conditions specified by the Minister, the Minister may delegate to any qualified person or class of persons any of the powers, duties or functions the Minister is authorized to exercise or perform for the purposes of this Part."

This indicates that the Minister retains the authority to delegate, but this delegation is subject to conditions set by the Minister. The delegation can be made to either a specific qualified person or to a class of persons.

### Section 140(2): Delegation to Provincial Bodies

Section 140(2) specifically addresses delegation to provincial bodies.
"Subject to subsection (3), the Minister may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, enter into an agreement with any province or any provincial body specifying the terms and conditions under which the Minister may delegate to a person employed by that province or provincial body the powers, duties or functions that the Minister or the Head is authorized to exercise or perform for the purposes of this Part."

This section allows for delegation to individuals employed by a province or provincial body, but it requires approval from the Governor in Council and involves an agreement outlining the terms and conditions of the delegation.

### Section 140(5): Liability of Delegated Person

Section 140(5) clarifies the liability of individuals to whom powers are delegated.
"A person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) or (1.1), or under an agreement entered into under subsection (2), is not personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith in the actual or purported exercise of those powers or performance of those duties or functions."

This provision protects the delegated person from personal liability when acting in good faith within the scope of their delegated authority.

### Section 140(6): Crown's Liability
"Despite subsection (5), and for greater certainty, Her Majesty in right of Canada is not relieved of any civil liability to which Her Majesty in right of Canada may otherwise be subject."

This ensures that the Crown remains liable for any actions taken by a delegated person, even if the delegated person is protected from personal liability.

In summary, the Minister retains the power to delegate their authority under Section 140. This delegation can be made to qualified individuals or to provincial bodies, subject to certain conditions and approvals. The delegated person is shielded from personal liability when acting in good faith, but the Crown remains ultimately responsible.

question: What is the legislative intent behind the provision regarding proceedings under this Part of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Legislative Intent Regarding Proceedings Under This Part of the Canada Labour Code

The legislative intent behind the provisions regarding proceedings under this Part of the Canada Labour Code appears to be multifaceted, focusing on establishing a clear framework for addressing workplace offences, ensuring fairness and efficiency in the process, and providing avenues for redress. This analysis will explore the intent based on the provided sections.

### Limitation Period and Timeliness of Proceedings

Section 257(2) explicitly states:
"...in respect of an offence under this Part may be instituted at any time within but not later than three years after the time when the subject-matter of the proceedings arose."

This provision demonstrates a clear intent to establish a reasonable time limit for bringing complaints. The "three years" timeframe aims to balance the need to address offences promptly with the practical challenges of gathering evidence and ensuring accurate recall of events. The intent is to prevent stale claims while still allowing for thorough investigations.

### Restrictions on Proceedings Against Corporate Directors

Section 257(3) further clarifies the legislative intent by stipulating:
"No proceeding against a director of a corporation in respect of an offence under this Part shall be instituted except with the consent of the Minister."

This provision highlights a deliberate intent to provide a layer of oversight and accountability when proceedings involve corporate directors. The requirement for ministerial consent suggests a recognition of the potential impact of such proceedings and a desire to ensure that they are pursued judiciously and in the public interest. This could be to prevent frivolous lawsuits or to ensure that the focus remains on the underlying offences rather than solely on individual directors.

### Scope of Complaints and Information

Section 257(1) outlines the scope of complaints:
"A complaint or information under this Part may relate to one or more offences by one employer in respect of one or more of his employees."

This indicates an intent to create a comprehensive mechanism for addressing a range of workplace offences. The ability to bring complaints relating to multiple offences and multiple employees under the same employer suggests a desire to address systemic issues rather than focusing on isolated incidents.

### Ensuring Fair Compensation for Employee Attendance at Proceedings

Section 146.5, while not directly about initiating proceedings, is relevant to the overall intent by addressing the financial impact on employees involved. It states:
"An employee who is a party to a proceeding under subsection 146.1(1) and who attends at the proceeding, or any employee who has been summoned by the Board to attend at such a proceeding and who attends, is entitled to be paid by the employer at the employee’s regular rate of wages for the time spent at the proceeding that would otherwise have been time at work."

This provision demonstrates an intent to protect employees from financial hardship when participating in the legal process. By ensuring that employees are compensated for their time spent at proceedings, the Code aims to encourage participation and ensure fairness in the system.

### Regulation and Flexibility

Section 245 indicates the intent to allow for flexibility and adaptation of the regulations governing unjust dismissal complaints. It states:
"For the purposes of this Division, the Governor in Council may make regulations (a) defining the absences from employment that shall be deemed not to have interrupted continuity of employment; (b) prescribing circumstances for the purposes of paragraph 240(3)(b); (c) prescribing periods for the purposes of subsection 241(4); (d) prescribing the circumstances under which a complaint is not to be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 241(5); and (e) prescribing the conditions that are to be met before a complaint may be deemed to be withdrawn under subsection 241(5)."

This provision shows the intent to allow the government to adapt the regulations to address evolving workplace practices and ensure the fairness and effectiveness of the unjust dismissal process.

### Prohibition of Interference with Conciliation and Review Processes

Section 86 clearly states:
"No order shall be made, process entered or proceeding taken in any court (a) to question the appointment of, or refusal to appoint, a conciliation officer or conciliation commissioner, or the establishment of, or the refusal to establish, a conciliation board; or (b) to review, prohibit or restrain any proceeding of a conciliation officer, conciliation commissioner or conciliation board."

This provision demonstrates a strong intent to protect the conciliation and mediation processes. By prohibiting court interference with these processes, the Code aims to encourage amicable resolution of disputes and avoid unnecessary litigation. The intent is to prioritize alternative dispute resolution methods.

In summary, the legislative intent behind the provisions regarding proceedings under this Part of the Canada Labour Code is to create a balanced and effective system for addressing workplace offences, ensuring fairness to both employers and employees, promoting timely resolution of disputes, and encouraging alternative dispute resolution methods.

question: What is the intended effect of setting a time limit for the validity of regulations made under section 296 of the Canada Labour Code?
answer:
## Time Limits for Regulations Under Section 296 of the Canada Labour Code

### Purpose of the Time Limit

Section 296 of the Canada Labour Code grants the Governor in Council the authority to create regulations concerning pilot projects designed to improve compliance with Parts II and III of the Act. The inclusion of a time limit for the validity of these regulations, as detailed in CLC-111, serves a specific purpose.

### Duration and Implementation
"Unless they are repealed earlier, regulations made under section 263 are repealed on the fifth anniversary of the day on which they come into force." This passage from CLC-263 indicates that regulations made under section 263, which is similar in nature to section 296, are not intended to be permanent. They are subject to a sunset clause, expiring after five years from their enactment.

### Rationale Behind the Time Limit

The implementation of a time limit for regulations under section 296 likely aims to ensure that these regulations remain relevant and effective. 

The time limit allows for periodic review and reassessment of the pilot project regulations. This ensures that the regulations continue to align with the evolving needs of the labour market and the Act's objectives. 

Furthermore, the sunset clause promotes accountability and encourages the Governor in Council to regularly evaluate the success of pilot projects and the effectiveness of the regulations governing them. This prevents regulations from becoming outdated or unnecessary. 

The intention is to foster adaptability and responsiveness within the regulatory framework, allowing for adjustments based on experience and changing circumstances.

question: What happens to an employee's status under the Canada Labour Code if they cease to work due to a lockout or strike, or are dismissed contrary to the Code?
answer:
## Employee Status During and After Lockouts or Strikes

The Canada Labour Code outlines specific provisions regarding employee status during and after lockouts or strikes. Here's a breakdown based on the provided documents:

### Section 87.5: Rights Unaffected During Lockouts or Strikes

This section addresses the continuity of employment terms during a lockout or strike.

**Continuity of Employment Terms:
"Where the Board has received an application pursuant to subsection 87.4(4) or a question has been referred to the Board pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), the employer must not alter the rates of pay or any other term or condition of employment or any right or privilege of the employees in the bargaining unit, or any right or privilege of the bargaining agent, without the consent of the bargaining agent, until the later of the date on which the Board has determined the application or the question referred and the date on which the requirements of paragraphs 89(1)(a) to (d) have been met."

This indicates that during a lockout or strike, an employer cannot unilaterally change an employee's pay or working conditions without the bargaining agent's consent, provided certain conditions are met. This ensures that employees retain their existing rights and benefits during the dispute.

**Impact on Strike/Lockout:
"A referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(5), during a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, or an application or referral made pursuant to subsection 87.4(7), does not suspend the strike or lockout."

This clarifies that the initiation of a referral or application related to the strike or lockout does not halt the ongoing work stoppage.

### Section 87.6: Reinstatement of Employees After Strike or Lockout

This section specifically addresses the reinstatement of employees after a strike or lockout.

**Prioritized Reinstatement:
"At the end of a strike or lockout not prohibited by this Part, the employer must reinstate employees in the bargaining unit who were on strike or locked out, in preference to any other person."

This is a crucial provision. It mandates that upon the conclusion of a strike or lockout, employees who were participating in the work stoppage must be reinstated before any other individuals are considered for employment. This ensures that employees are prioritized for their jobs after the dispute is resolved.

In summary, the Canada Labour Code protects employees' rights and employment terms during lockouts and strikes, and guarantees their reinstatement after the work stoppage ends.

{"id": "LABOUR-REPORTS-7_61", "type": "canada.ca", "title": "Report of the Expert Panel on Modern Federal Labour Standards", "section": "N/A"}, "text": "**Anti-reprisal protection for  concerted activity** Studies  show that many workers are unlikely to speak out about problems in the  workplace if they do not have access to collective voice mechanisms because  they fear reprisal. This is particularly true for non-unionized workers and  those in non-standard work, as well as women. For instance, using survey  data collected in 2005, Lewchuk (2013) concludes that "the precariously  employed were six to seven times more likely to report that raising health and  safety issues would have negative employment consequences".  In the United States, section 7 of the National Labor  Relations Act (NLRA) provides non-supervisory employees, both union and  non-union, with the right to engage in "concerted activity for the purpose of  collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection". As defined by the  U.S. Supreme Court, "mutual aid and protection" includes employees’ efforts to  "improve current terms and conditions of employment or otherwise improve their  lots as employees through channels outside the immediate employee/employer  relationship"Footnote 135 The Act does not limit the manner, time or place in which  employees engage in "concerted activity". While section 7 lists workers’ protected rights, section 8 makes it  unlawful for an employer to "interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in  the exercise of the rights guaranteed in section 7". The employer’s conduct will be considered as retaliation if  it tends to interfere with the free exercise of employee rights under the NLRA  and "demonstrating motive or actual coercion is therefore not generally  required" (Rogers & Archer, 2016). Sections 7 and 8 were introduced  when the NLRA was enacted in 1935.  Section 7 of the NLRA protects concerted activities by  unionized workers and non-unionized workers, whether they are seeking to  unionize or not (Rogers & Archer, 2016). The spectrum of protected  concerted activities is wide and includes concerted complaints or grievances  presented to employers regarding compensation, benefits or working conditions,  as well as informal discussions between employees about their working  conditions (Fullerton & Millman, 2008). The protected activities must generally be undertaken by two or more  employees seeking to improve their terms or conditions of employment.  Thus, two or more employees addressing their employer about  improving their pay will be exercising their right to protected concerted  activity. However, the  protection can also extend to the actions of one employee, on the condition  that such actions have "the object of initiating or inducing or preparing  for group action or [have] some relation to group action in the interest of the  employees." Footnote 136 Footnote 137 Section 7 will apply when an  employee speaks to his employer on behalf of one or more co-workers about  improving workplace conditions (NLRB, n.d.). Non-union work stoppages and  walkouts are generally protected,Footnote 138 unless they are "unlawful, violent, […] in breach of contract [or]  "irresponsible" because they threaten property damage" (Rogers & Archer,  2016). Section 7 has been interpreted to  extend the "Weingarten" rule (that is, that an employee in a  unionized workplace may request the presence of a union representative at an  investigatory interview which employee reasonably believes might result in  disciplinary action) to cover employees in non-union workplaces.Footnote 139 The use of social media is, to a  certain extent, protected by section 7 as employees have the right to address  work-related issues and share information about pay, benefits, and working  conditions with coworkers on Facebook, YouTube, and other social media. To be  protected, the use of social media must have some relation to group action, or  seek to initiate, induce or prepare for group action, or bring a group  complaint to the attention of management (Neylon O’Brien, 2011; Bemberg, 2018).  For  instance, an employer's decision to  dismiss an employee who posted a comment on Facebook encouraging a terminated  colleague to hire a lawyer and sue the company was over-ruled by the National  Labor Relations Board (NLRB). The Facebook comment was found to be a protected concerted activity  that did not interfere with the employer’s operations.Footnote 140 However, complaints that are made  publicly and are maliciously false will not be protected.Footnote 141 Many employers have social media policies that aim to limit what their  employee may publish. When such policies are found to be overly broad (that is,  when they prohibit lawful activities either explicitly or by being too vague),  the NLRB can order the employer to rescind or modify them.Footnote 142 Protected  concerted activities provide statutory protection against reprisals for  employees wishing to collectively voice concerns. This form of collective voice  is independent from the employer who is required to not interfere. The American  experience suggests that it can be useful in circumstances in which employees  face particularly egregious working conditions and are otherwise unable to  bring about change or improvements.  For  example, in a leading 1962 case (NLRB v. Washington  Aluminum) workers had  complained about the cold temperatures in the facility during the winter. Footnote 143 On a particularly cold day workers arrived to  find the plant completely unheated and seven walked out. The U.S. Supreme Court  upheld the NLRB’s ruling that the company’s termination of these workers was  unlawful. Similarly, in a more recent case a group of restaurant workers who  had been terminated after protesting working conditions appealed to the NLRB  which ordered them reinstated (Greenhouse, 2015). A search on Lexis Advance US conducted in March  2019 yielded 8,993 NLRB cases dealing with section 7, going back as far as  1935. Although this is a small number over a period of more than 80 years, the  number of cases per year has grown substantially in recent years during a time  when private sector unionization has also fallen sharply. Figure 18  plots  the number of cases per year over the 1935 to 2019 period. The number has  increased significantly over the past two decades.   Figure 18: Number of cases before the NLRB  (section 7 NLRA), 1935–2019   Figure 18 - Text version    Dates Number of cases   1935–1939 396   1940–1944 487   1945–1949 24   1950–1954 42   1955–1959 45   1960–1964 102   1965–1969 187   1970–1974 430   1975-1979 916   1980–1984 854   1985–1989 445   1990–1994 443   1995–1999 329   2000–2004 335   2005-2009 753   2010–2014 1806   2015–2019 1565      Source:  Panel analysis of NLRB/Lexis Advance US.    However, it is important to note that the number of cases  related to section 7 is likely to understate the importance of this provision  because of the "threat effect"—employers who are aware of the law and previous  interpretations by the courts will adjust their behaviour in order to be in  compliance and avoid a costly lawsuit.  Unlike some other  mechanisms, the NLRA protection for concerted activity has the advantage of  having been available and used in the United States, a country that shares many  commonalities with Canada’s labour relations system. It is unclear whether the  collective voice achievable with the support of such a protection might develop  into more sustained collective activity, such as achieving union  representation. Nevertheless, adopting a protection for concerted activity  might be helpful for workers in the FRPS with particularly poor working  conditions.  Recommendation 25: The Panel recommends introducing  a protection for concerted activities in Part III of the Code.  Our recommendation regarding  this protection is two-fold. First, Part III should state that employees have a  right to participate in concerted activities. Second, employees  who have been dismissed,  suspended, laid-off, demoted or otherwise disciplined because they have  exercised their right to concerted activity should be protected against such  reprisals.Footnote 144 Adding a protection for  concerted activity to Part III would also likely enhance workers’  willingness to join participatory initiatives channelled through community  organizations. The Panel views this right as a potentially useful incremental  change to Canada’s labour relations system in the FRPS and one that would bring  the Code more in line with recent Supreme Court interpretations of the  guarantee of freedom of association in section 2(d) of the Canadian Charter of  Rights and Freedoms."

question: How does the Canada Labour Code ensure that the rights provided under the Canadian Human Rights Act are protected in the context of employment relationships?
answer:
## Protection of Canadian Human Rights Act Rights within Employment Relationships under the Canada Labour Code

### Section 123.1 of the Canada Labour Code

The Canada Labour Code explicitly ensures the protection of rights provided under the Canadian Human Rights Act. Section 123.1 states:
"For greater certainty, nothing in this Part shall be construed so as to abrogate or derogate from the rights provided for under the Canadian Human Rights Act..."

This statement is a fundamental principle within the Labour Code. It signifies that the provisions of the Labour Code, including those related to employment standards and workplace rights, cannot be interpreted in a way that diminishes or eliminates the protections offered by the Canadian Human Rights Act. This ensures that individuals are safeguarded against discrimination based on grounds such as race, religion, gender, age, or disability, even within the context of their employment.

### Section 123.3: Burden of Proof in Human Rights-Related Proceedings

Furthermore, Section 123.3 addresses the burden of proof in proceedings related to the Canadian Human Rights Act within the Labour Code framework. It specifies:
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, or in any proceeding under Part IV in respect of a violation that is related to this Part, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

This provision is crucial for protecting individuals who may face discrimination or other human rights violations in the workplace. By placing the burden of proof on the employer when contesting an employment relationship, the Code aims to prevent employers from misclassifying employees to avoid their obligations under the Canadian Human Rights Act. This ensures that individuals who believe their human rights have been violated have a fairer opportunity to demonstrate the true nature of their employment relationship.

### Recommendation 25: Introducing a Protection for Concerted Activities

The Panel recommends introducing a protection for concerted activities in Part III of the Code. This recommendation aims to further strengthen the rights of employees and align the Code with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
"The Panel recommends introducing  a protection for concerted activities in Part III of the Code.  Our recommendation regarding  this protection is two-fold. First, Part III should state that employees have a  right to participate in concerted activities. Second, employees  who have been dismissed,  suspended, laid-off, demoted or otherwise disciplined because they have  exercised their right to concerted activity should be protected against such..."

This proposed addition would provide a legal framework for employees to collectively address workplace concerns, including those related to human rights. By protecting employees from retaliation for engaging in concerted activities, the Code would empower them to advocate for better working conditions and challenge discriminatory practices.

question: What protections are afforded to the Head and those delegated authority under the Canada Labour Code when carrying out their duties and functions?
answer:
## Protections for the Head and Delegated Authority

### Section 249(8): Immunity from Liability

Section 249(8) explicitly states:
"Neither the Head nor a person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1) is personally liable for anything done or omitted to be done by them in good faith under the authority or purported authority of this Part."

This provision offers significant protection. It shields both the Head and those to whom they delegate authority from personal liability if they act in good faith while performing their duties under the Canada Labour Code. This means that even if errors are made or actions have unintended consequences, individuals are not personally responsible, as long as they acted honestly and with the intention of fulfilling their responsibilities.

### Section 249(6): Protection from Testimony

Section 249(6) provides a further layer of protection by stating:
"The Head shall not be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions."

This means the Head cannot be compelled to testify in legal proceedings about information gathered while performing their duties under the Labour Code. This protection is intended to ensure that the Head can carry out their responsibilities without fear of being forced to disclose confidential information or potentially incriminating details.

Furthermore, Section 249(7) extends this protection to those who have assisted the Head. It states:
"No person to whom powers, duties or functions have been delegated under subsection (1), and no person who has accompanied or assisted such a person or the Head in carrying out their duties and functions, shall be required to give testimony in any civil suit or civil proceedings, or in any proceeding under section 242, with regard to information obtained in carrying out those duties and functions or in accompanying or assisting the person, except with the written permission of the Head."

This ensures that individuals assisting the Head are also protected from being compelled to testify about information obtained during the performance of duties, unless the Head specifically grants permission. This protection is crucial for maintaining the integrity of investigations and ensuring that individuals can assist without fear of legal repercussions.
