question: In cases where an employee complains about an employer's action related to certain rights, who bears the burden of proof to demonstrate that the alleged contravention did or did not occur?
answer:
## Burden of Proof in Employee Complaints Regarding Employer Actions

This analysis examines the burden of proof in cases where an employee complains about an employer's actions related to certain rights, drawing from the provided Canada Labour Code sections.

### Section 133 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 133 directly addresses the burden of proof in complaints made to the Board.

**Complaint Process and Burden of Proof
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This passage is crucial. It establishes a specific rule:
"...if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party." This means that if an employer disputes the employee's claim that a violation occurred when the employee is exercising a right under sections 128 or 129, the employer must prove that the violation did not happen.

### Section 6.2 of the Canada Labour Code

Section 6.2 outlines the burden of proof when an employer alleges that a person is not their employee.

**Burden of Proof in Employment Status Disputes
"If, in any proceeding under this Part other than a prosecution, an employer alleges that a person is not their employee, the burden of proof is on the employer."

While not directly related to complaints about actions related to rights, this section highlights a general principle: "the burden of proof is on the employer" when disputing an employee's employment status. This principle suggests a broader tendency to place the onus on the employer to demonstrate wrongdoing or a lack of a specific condition.

### Section 133(6) - Reinforcement of Burden of Proof

Section 133(6) reinforces the burden of proof on the party alleging non-occurrence of a violation.

**Evidence of Contravention
"A complaint made under this section in respect of the exercise of a right under section 128 or 129 is itself evidence that the contravention actually occurred and, if a party to the complaint proceedings alleges that the contravention did not occur, the burden of proof is on that party."

This reiterates the point made in section 133, emphasizing that the complaint itself serves as evidence, and the onus is on the party denying the violation to prove it did not occur.

In summary, when an employee complains about an employer's action related to certain rights, the burden of proof rests on the employer to demonstrate that the alleged contravention did not occur, particularly when the employee is exercising a right under sections 128 or 129.

question: Under what conditions can the maximum hours of work for an employee in a week be adjusted or have exceptions?
answer:
## Adjusting and Exception to Maximum Hours of Work

### Emergency Work
"In case of emergency, such as an accident or essential work on equipment, an employer may exceed the maximum hours of work without a permit." This indicates that the standard maximum hours can be temporarily exceeded when unforeseen emergencies arise. 

### Averaging Hours
"In some establishments, the nature of work necessitates irregular hours of work due to seasonal or other factors. This means that as an employee, you may be subject to:   scheduled hours that vary from time to time, or no regularly scheduled hours  If this applies to you, your employer may average your hours of work over a period of 2 or more weeks." This allows for flexibility in work schedules when the workload is not consistent throughout the week. Instead of adhering to a strict daily or weekly limit, the hours are calculated over a longer period.

### Excess Hour Permit
"...the maximum hours of work can be exceeded:  under an excess hour permit  for emergency work..." This is a specific mechanism for allowing work beyond the standard limit, but it is restricted to emergency situations.

### Modified Work Schedule
"Modified work schedules may provide you and your employer with greater flexibility in the workplace as they allow employees to work outside the standard hours of work." This allows for a variety of work arrangements that deviate from the standard schedule, potentially impacting the maximum hours.

### Exemptions for Certain Classes of Employees
"Regulations set out exemptions from or modifications to what maximum hours of work is for certain classes of employees:  drivers in the trucking industry (Motor Vehicle Operators Hours of Work Regulations) employees on ships in the East Coast and Great Lakes shipping industry (East Coast and Great Lakes Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations, 1985) and the West Coast shipping industry (West Coast Shipping Employees Hours of Work Regulations) running trades employees in the railway industry (Railway Running-Trades Employees Hours of Work Regulations) the commission salespersons in the broadcasting industry (Broadcasting Industry Commission Salesmen Hours of Work Regulations), and the commission-paid salespeople in the banking industry (Banking Industry Commission-paid Salespeople Hours of Work Regulations)..." This highlights that certain professions are subject to different rules regarding maximum hours.

### Collective Agreement and Approval
"Section 172 (1) An employer may, in respect of one or more employees subject to a collective agreement, establish, modify or cancel a work schedule under which the hours exceed the maximum set out in section 171 or in regulations made under section 175 if (a) the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks does not exceed forty-eight hours a week; and (b) the schedule, or its modification or cancellation, is agreed to in writing by the employer and the trade union." This indicates that under a collective agreement, the maximum hours can be adjusted if agreed upon by both the employer and the union, provided the average hours over two weeks do not exceed 48.
"Subject to subsection (3), an employer may, in respect of one or more employees not subject to a collective agreement, establish, modify or cancel a work schedule under which the hours exceed the maximum set out in section 171 or in regulations made under section 175 if (a) the average hours of work for a period of two or more weeks does not exceed forty-eight hours a week; and (b) the schedule, or its modification or cancellation, has been approved (i) in the case of one employee’s schedule, in writing by that employee, or (ii) in the case of more than one employee’s schedule, by at least 70% of the affected employees." This allows for adjustments to the maximum hours even without a collective agreement, but requires either individual employee approval or approval from a significant majority of affected employees.
